nuance.analogy: A survivable outcome is like a rough landing: it hurts and leaves marks, but you walk away from it.
nuance.etymology: From survive, from Latin supervivere 'to live beyond,' with the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Using the nonstandard form survivalable instead of survivable.
Using survivable in everyday speech to mean bearable, where tolerable or 'I can handle it' fits better.

senses.definition: A group whose elements are precisely all of the bijections of some set with itself and whose operation is composition of those bijections.
senses.example: In group theory, the symmetric group on n letters consists of all permutations of those letters.

core.definition: In group theory, the group of all one-to-one mappings of a set onto itself, with composition as the operation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'MEH' in 'symmetric' and on 'GROOP' in 'group', which is a long 'oo' sound. Keep the first syllable weak, like 'suh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in abstract algebra.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians say this phrase in courses, papers and talks on abstract algebra. The phrase is almost always spoken in a technical setting, and Americans often shorten it in conversation to 'the symmetric group on n letters.' No casual everyday use exists.

distinctions.note: A symmetric group is a permutation group on all elements of a set, so the two terms overlap but the symmetric group is the full version.
A cyclic group is generated by a single element; the symmetric group is typically much larger and not cyclic.

collocations: the symmetric group on n letters

examples.everyday: My son is studying for a math exam and keeps talking about the symmetric group, which I don't really understand.
examples.professional: For this cryptography project, we model the permutations as elements of the symmetric group and check closure.
examples.analytical: The symmetric group on a finite set is the paradigm example of a non-abelian group, which makes it central to the theory of permutations.

nuance.analogy: Like the set of every way to shuffle a deck of cards, where each shuffle is an action you can combine.
nuance.etymology: 'Symmetric' from Greek summetria; 'group' from Italian gruppo, a band or cluster.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'symmetric' on the first syllable; the main stress falls on the second syllable.
Confusing the symmetric group with symmetry as a general property; in math it has a precise meaning.

senses.definition: Additions to the syntax of a programming language that make code easier for humans to read or write, but that do not change the functionality or expressiveness of the language.
senses.example: In fact, this is how lists are actually built, by consing all elements to the empty list, []. The commas-and-brackets notation is just syntactic sugar, a more pleasant way to write code. So [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] is exactly equivalent to 1:2:3:4:5:[].

core.definition: Language features that make code easier to write or read but add no new capability, since the same result can be achieved another way.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress in syntactic is on TAK, and sugar stresses SHOO. Say 'sugar' with an American r at the end, and don't let the 'ug' turn into 'oo' or 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly positive. It implies a convenience that makes code more pleasant to write, but it can sound dismissive if someone says it is 'just' syntactic sugar.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use syntactic sugar mainly among programmers, in code reviews, language design discussions, and developer blogs. Saying a feature is 'just syntactic sugar' implies it adds no real power, so it can sound like a mild criticism. In casual talk outside tech, people would not use the phrase.

distinctions.note: Syntax is the set of grammatical rules of a language; syntactic sugar is a feature built on top of those rules for convenience.
A library function adds a new capability to a program, while syntactic sugar changes only how code is written and does not add expressiveness.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the new shortcut in the app is basically syntactic sugar, so it doesn't change what the app can do.
examples.professional: That new shorthand for async calls is just syntactic sugar, so I'm fine approving it if the tests still pass.
examples.analytical: Whether a construct counts as syntactic sugar depends on whether it can be translated mechanically into existing syntax without changing what the language can express.

nuance.analogy: Like a sugar-coated pill: it makes the thing easier to swallow, but the medicine inside is the same.
nuance.etymology: Coined by computer scientist Peter Landin in the 1960s to describe convenient notation that adds no new meaning.
common_mistakes: Confusing syntactic sugar with syntax itself; syntax is the grammar, and syntactic sugar is a convenience built on it.
Mispronouncing sugar as SHUG-ar or SHOO-gar; the American form is SHOO-ger.

senses.definition: A system of mode or procedure.
senses.example: scare tactics

senses.definition: The military science that deals with achieving the objectives set by strategy.
senses.example: The cadets spent the semester studying tactics, from small-unit movement to battlefield coordination.

senses.definition: The employment and ordered arrangement of forces in relation to each other.
senses.example: The general changed his tactics after scouts reported the enemy's flanks were exposed.

core.definition: Planned methods or moves used to achieve a specific goal, especially in sports, business, politics or war.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Keep the final -cs as a clear 'ks' sound; do not add a vowel between k and s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word can be positive, as in good tactics, or negative, as in dirty tactics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually treat 'tactics' as plural, as in 'their tactics were effective,' even when the subject is a single field, though 'tactics is' appears in technical writing. The phrase 'dirty tactics' is common and suggests unfair methods. In sports talk, 'tactics' often means a team's formation or game plan.

distinctions.note: Strategy is the overall plan; tactics are the specific actions used to carry it out.
Techniques are skills or methods of doing a task well; tactics are planned moves aimed at a rival or obstacle.

examples.everyday: The kids used sneaky tactics to get out of cleaning their room, but Mom saw right through them.
examples.professional: Our tactics for the product launch focus on early customer feedback before we commit to a full rollout.
examples.analytical: The essay examines the tactics of persuasion, showing how rhetoric shapes the public's sense of what is reasonable.

nuance.analogy: Tactics are like the individual notes in a song: strategy is the melody, and tactics are the specific notes played to bring it to life.
nuance.etymology: Plural of tactic, from Greek taktika, 'the art of arranging', from taktikos.
common_mistakes: Using 'tactics' as a singular noun in everyday speech, as in 'this tactics is good'; say 'this tactic' for one method.
Confusing 'tactics' with 'tactic' when referring to a single planned move.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or similar to, a talisman.
Possessing or believed to possess protective magical power.

core.definition: Of or relating to a talisman; having or seeming to have protective magical power or lucky influence.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MAN, with a short 'a' as in 'cat' rather than 'ah.' The first syllable has a secondary stress, and the '-ic' ending is 'ik,' not 'eek.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests that someone or something has a special, almost magical power to bring protection or success.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use talismanic mostly in writing, journalism and sports commentary, for example describing a star player whose presence seems to bring luck. In casual speech people more often say 'lucky charm' or 'good luck charm.' Using it for ordinary objects sounds overly dramatic unless you mean they really seem magical.

distinctions.note: Magical is a broad word for anything with supernatural qualities, while talismanic specifically refers to something that seems to protect or bring luck.
Symbolic means representing an idea, while talismanic adds the belief that the thing actively protects or brings good fortune.
An amulet is a noun for a worn object with protective power, while talismanic is the adjective describing that kind of power.

examples.everyday: Our shortstop is so talismanic that the team seems to play better whenever he's in the lineup.
examples.professional: The investors treated the founder as a talismanic figure, even though the product roadmap was still thin.
examples.analytical: Some historians describe the relic as talismanic, a source of protection rather than merely a reminder of faith.

nuance.analogy: A talismanic object works like a lucky penny in a pocket: its value lies in what people believe it does.
nuance.etymology: From Arabic ṭilsam, borrowed into European languages through French or Italian talisman; it is often linked to Greek telesma, meaning consecrated object.
common_mistakes: Using talismanic as a noun; the noun is talisman.
Stressing the first syllable only, or pronouncing the middle as 'iz-MAN' with a long vowel.
Confusing it with talented, which means having ability, not magical power.

senses.definition: The property of being tangible.
senses.example: The tangibility of the gold coins reassured investors who distrusted digital assets.

senses.definition: Something that is tangible.
senses.example: The prototype offered a tangibility the team's abstract plans had lacked for months.

core.definition: The quality of being real, concrete, or clearly perceptible, so that something can be touched, measured, or clearly seen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable -BIL, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. The -ble is 'buh', and the final -ity is 'uh-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests that something is concrete and real, and in business it can imply accountability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tangibility in business, philosophy, and marketing, for example 'the tangibility of results' or 'a lack of tangibility'. In everyday speech they usually say 'something you can actually see or touch'. The word is more common in writing than in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Concreteness means specific and definite; tangibility focuses on whether something can be touched, measured, or clearly perceived.
Reality means existence; tangibility means that existence is clearly perceptible or measurable.

examples.everyday: After all the planning, the new kitchen finally gave the house a real sense of tangibility.
examples.professional: Leadership asked for more tangibility in the quarterly goals, so we added measurable milestones.
examples.analytical: Hume's empiricism demands a standard of tangibility that many metaphysical claims cannot meet.

nuance.analogy: Like a receipt you can hold in your hand, as opposed to a promise you only heard over the phone.
nuance.etymology: From tangible, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tangere, to touch, with the suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Confusing tangibility with tangent or tangential, which share the root but have different meanings.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'tan-juh-BIL-ih-tee' with a different vowel; the main stress is on -BIL.

core.definition: A major ancient city in Cilicia, in what is now southern Turkey, and the birthplace of the apostle Paul.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is a reduced uh sound, so say it quickly as 'sus'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical and biblical place name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear Tarsus in Bible classes, church history and sermons about Paul. In normal conversation it is rarely used, and people usually add context, such as 'Paul was from Tarsus.' It is a city name, so it is always capitalized.

distinctions.note: Tarsus is a city in Cilicia associated with Paul, while Tarshish is a distant place linked with ships and Jonah.

examples.everyday: My friend said Paul was born in Tarsus, which is in modern Turkey.
examples.professional: The mission report noted that the early church spread quickly from Antioch and Tarsus.
examples.analytical: Paul's identity as a man of Tarsus illuminates his Hellenistic and Jewish background.

nuance.analogy: Tarsus is like a hometown that shapes a person's identity, even after they travel the world.
nuance.etymology: Ancient Greek Tarsos, the name of the city in Cilicia.
common_mistakes: Confusing Tarsus with Tarshish.
Stressing the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Tarsus was a major city in Cilicia and the hometown of the apostle Paul. Acts 9:11 mentions a man of Tarsus named Saul, and Acts 21:39 has Paul say he is a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia. Acts 22:3 says Paul was born at Tarsus and was educated in Jerusalem.

senses.definition: A fear of new technologies.

core.definition: An intense or irrational fear of, or strong dislike for, new technologies, computers, and complicated machines.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TEK. The -bia ending is pronounced bee-uh with the final vowel reduced, not as bi-a with a hard i. Keep the oh in both -no- and -fo- as long o sounds.

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing a fear or avoidance. People often use it lightly or about themselves in a self-deprecating way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in casual conversation and in workplace talk about older employees, parents, or people learning software. Saying 'I have technophobia' can sound light and friendly, but calling someone a technophobe may sound like a mild insult. A natural reply is 'Ha, same, I just need someone to show me how it works.'

distinctions.note: Technophobia is the noun for the fear itself, while technophobic is the adjective used to describe a person or reaction.
A Luddite is someone who opposes new technology on principle, often with historical or political reasons. Technophobia describes a personal fear or discomfort and is less political.

examples.everyday: My mom has a bit of technophobia, so she still calls me every time her email stops working.
examples.professional: Some of our senior staff show real technophobia, so the training needs hands-on sessions instead of videos.
examples.analytical: The rise of technophobia in mid-century critiques reflected deeper worries about automation and loss of human control.

nuance.analogy: It's like claustrophobia, but the closed space is a smartphone, a computer, or any new machine.
nuance.etymology: From techno-, from Greek tekhnē 'art, skill', and -phobia, from Greek phobos 'fear'.
common_mistakes: Using 'technophobia' as an adjective, as in 'technophobia people'; the correct adjective is 'technophobic'.
Pronouncing the stress on the -pho- syllable instead of the first syllable.

core.definition: Having ten strings, used especially of the ancient Hebrew stringed instrument named in the Psalms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'TEN' in this compound adjective. The 'ng' is a single sound, and the final 'ed' is pronounced as a 'd' after the nasal, so it sounds like 'TEN-strind'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive, biblical or poetic term, not used in everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly use this word in Bible study, hymns, poetry, and academic writing about ancient music. In a modern conversation, you would more often say 'a harp with ten strings' or 'a lyre'. It is rare outside religious and literary contexts.

distinctions.note: Stringed is the general term for instruments with strings; ten-stringed specifies the number.
A lyre is a type of stringed instrument; ten-stringed describes a particular kind of lyre or harp.

examples.everyday: The pastor said the psalm was written for a ten-stringed instrument, so I looked up what that might have sounded like.
examples.professional: The music curriculum includes a short lesson on reconstructing ancient instruments, including the ten-stringed lyre described in some psalms.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the ten-stringed instrument of Psalm 33 refers to a harp, a lyre, or a psaltery, since the Hebrew term is uncertain.

nuance.analogy: A ten-stringed instrument is like a guitar with ten strings instead of six: the number tells you exactly what kind of sound to expect.
nuance.etymology: Compound of ten and stringed, from Old English strenge 'string'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'ten string' without the -ed ending when used as an adjective.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'ten-STRINGED'.
Using it for modern instruments such as a ten-string guitar, which is rare.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew term is nevel 'asor, usually rendered as a ten-stringed instrument, often a harp or lyre. Psalm 33:2 invites praise with the harp of ten strings, and Psalm 144:9 mentions a ten-stringed instrument in a song of thanksgiving. The exact instrument is uncertain, but it was a prominent instrument in temple worship.

senses.definition: One who holds a lease (a tenancy).
senses.example: The tenant signed a twelve-month lease and moved in on the first of May.

senses.definition: One who has possession of any place.
senses.example: The tenant of the storage unit left the keys with the manager.

senses.definition: Any of a number of customers serviced through the same instance of an application.
senses.example: multi-tenant hosting

senses.definition: One who holds a feudal tenure in real property.
senses.example: Under the charter, every tenant owed the lord military service and a share of the harvest.

senses.definition: Misconstruction of tenet.
senses.example: Her essay argued that the church's core tenant of grace had been badly misread.

senses.definition: One who owns real estate other than via allodial title.
senses.example: Because the estate was held from the crown, the family were tenants rather than outright owners of the land.

senses.definition: To hold as, or be, a tenant.
senses.example: The company agreed to tenant the third floor of the office building.

senses.definition: To inhabit.
senses.example: Three families tenant the old farmhouse at the end of our road.

core.definition: A person who rents a house, apartment, office, or land from a landlord and pays rent for the right to use it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa, so the word has two syllables, 'TEN-unt', not 'TEN-ant'. Do not confuse it with 'tenet', which is pronounced 'TEN-it'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a role in a rental relationship, with legal rights and responsibilities.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tenant in housing, real estate, and legal contexts, often as 'the tenant' in a lease. In casual speech, people often say 'renter' or 'the person who rents'. Landlords and tenants have legal duties, and the term is used in formal notices.

distinctions.note: Renter is the everyday term; tenant is more formal and legal, often used in leases and housing law.
Lessee is a legal term for someone who leases property; tenant is the common term in housing.
Occupant is anyone living in a place, whether or not they pay rent; tenant implies a rental agreement.

examples.everyday: Our new tenant downstairs is really friendly, and she brought us cookies on her first day.
examples.professional: Each tenant in the building must submit a maintenance request through the property management portal.
examples.analytical: The legal status of the tenant depends on whether the agreement creates a tenancy or only a license to occupy.

nuance.analogy: A tenant is like a guest who pays for the room and keeps it clean, but does not own the house.
nuance.etymology: From Old French tenant, present participle of tenir, from Latin tenere 'to hold'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'ant' vowel, when it should be reduced.
Confusing tenant with tenet, which means a principle or belief.
Using tenant to describe someone who owns property.

tenant.etymology: From Middle English *tenaunt*, from Anglo-Norman *tenaunt* and Old French *tenant*, present participle of *tenir* (“to hold”), from Latin *teneō* (“hold, keep”).

conversation.text: The tenant upstairs plays music really late.
As a tenant, you have the right to a working heater.
The previous tenants left the apartment spotless.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to tension.
Capable of being stretched; ductile.
senses.example: Engineers tested the tensile strength of the cable before approving the bridge design.

core.definition: Relating to tension in a material, or able to be stretched a long way without breaking.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Keep the vowel short, as in 'ten', and do not stretch it into 'tane'. The final syllable is a short, light 'il'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used to describe physical properties, and it has no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers, scientists and materials experts use this word most often, as in 'tensile strength'. Ordinary Americans would more likely say 'stretchy' or 'strong' in casual talk. Use it in reports, specifications and technical discussions.

distinctions.note: Elastic describes a material that returns to its original shape after stretching, while tensile describes how much pulling force a material can take before it breaks.
Ductile means a material can be drawn out into a wire or thin shape without breaking, a property that is related to tensile behavior but is not the same thing.

examples.everyday: My neighbor said the new fishing line has great tensile strength, so it won't snap when he reels in a big one.
examples.professional: Before we approve the bridge cable, the lab needs to run a tensile test to confirm it can handle the load.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the tensile character of the argument, stretched between two opposing claims, is what keeps it from collapsing into either extreme.

nuance.analogy: A tensile material is like a rubber band that holds on under pull; its tensile strength is the point just before it snaps.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tensilis, from tendere, 'to stretch'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'TEN-sile' with a long i at the end, when the final syllable is short and light.
Using 'tensile' to mean 'tense' in the sense of nervous or stressed.

senses.definition: The process of terminating or the state of being terminated.
The process of firing an employee; ending one's employment at a business for any reason.
senses.example: After the layoffs, the company's termination of Sarah's position surprised her entire team.

senses.definition: An end in time; a conclusion.
senses.example: The lease's termination date came and went, so the tenants had to move out.

senses.definition: An end in space; an edge or limit.
senses.example: The hikers stopped at the termination of the trail, where the forest met open water.

senses.definition: An outcome or result.
senses.example: The experiment's termination produced results nobody on the team had predicted.

senses.definition: The last part of a word.
senses.example: In 'quickly,' the termination ly turns the adjective into an adverb.

senses.definition: An induced abortion.
senses.example: The clinic reported that every termination was performed by a licensed physician.

senses.definition: The ending up of a polypeptide chain.
senses.example: During translation, the ribosome releases the protein once the termination codon is reached.

core.definition: The act of ending something, such as a contract, a job, or a process, or the state of having ended.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -NAY-, and the ending -tion is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'. Many learners stress the first syllable out of habit, but the stress moves to the middle syllable because of the suffix.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in legal and technical contexts, but negative when it refers to someone losing their job, since it sounds impersonal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use termination in contracts, HR policies, and business emails, for example 'termination notice' or 'termination date'. In everyday conversation, people usually say 'firing' or 'getting let go' instead. In a medical context, the word can also refer to ending a pregnancy, which is a sensitive topic, so be careful with it in general conversation.

distinctions.note: Expiration means something ends by reaching its natural limit, such as a date, while termination means someone or something ends it before or by decision.
Resignation is when an employee chooses to leave, while termination is when the employer ends the employment.

examples.everyday: My landlord sent a termination notice, so we have sixty days to find a new place.
examples.professional: Please send HR the termination paperwork by Friday so payroll can process the final check.
examples.analytical: The termination of the study was justified not by its results but by the funding body's changing priorities.

nuance.analogy: Termination is like pulling the plug on a machine: the process stops, and it does not simply run down on its own.
nuance.etymology: From Latin terminatio, 'a limiting or ending', from terminare 'to end'.
common_mistakes: Using 'termination' in casual conversation about a job, which sounds cold; 'getting fired' is more natural.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'TER-mi-na-tion'; the stress belongs on -NAY-.

senses.definition: Something intermediate between two classifications.
A third party in a situation, such as one who comes between two potential romantic partners; a "gooseberry" or "third wheel".
senses.example: I felt like a tertium quid on their date, constantly hovering between them as the awkward third wheel.

core.definition: Something intermediate that does not fit neatly into either of two categories, or a third person who comes between two others.

pronunciation.tip: This is Latin used in English, so stress the first word on TUR and the second on KWID. Pronounce the final 'quid' as 'kwid,' not 'kwee-dee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an intellectual phrase used to name an in-between category, often with a light or humorous tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tertium quid' in academic writing, philosophy, law, and literary essays, not in casual speech. In everyday talk, people say 'third wheel' or 'gooseberry' for a third person who intrudes on a couple. A natural reply to someone who uses it is a clarifying question such as 'What is the third option?'

distinctions.note: 'Third wheel' is informal American slang for an unwanted third person in a couple. 'Tertium quid' is more formal and can refer to any intermediate category.
'Intermediate' is a plain English word for in-between. 'Tertium quid' is more specialized and suggests a third thing that resists classification.

collocations: neither one nor the other tertium quid

examples.everyday: Honestly, I felt like a third wheel at dinner, so I was almost a tertium quid between my sister and her fiancé.
examples.professional: The proposal treats the hybrid model as a tertium quid, neither fully centralized nor fully distributed.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean suggests a tertium quid between excess and deficiency rather than a simple choice between two extremes.

nuance.analogy: A tertium quid is like a color that is neither black nor white but gray, lying between two clear categories.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tertium quid, literally third something.
common_mistakes: Using it as a casual phrase in everyday conversation, where it sounds overly academic.
Pronouncing 'quid' as 'kwee-dee' instead of 'kwid.'

senses.definition: Synonym of too bad.
senses.example: You couldn't make the concert? Well, that's a shame.

core.definition: Said to express sympathy or mild disappointment about bad news or an unfortunate situation; it means the same as 'too bad'.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SHAME, with a long ay vowel. The 'a' is a weak uh, so the phrase flows as 'thats-uh-SHAYM'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative but sympathetic. It acknowledges disappointment without much drama, though a flat tone can sound sarcastic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in casual conversation when someone reports a cancellation, a loss, or a missed chance, such as 'You can't come to the barbecue?' It sounds warm when your voice shows real sympathy. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I was really looking forward to it,' or 'Maybe next time.'

distinctions.note: The two are almost interchangeable; that's a shame sounds a little warmer and more personal.
Ashamed describes your own guilt or embarrassment, while that's a shame comments on someone else's bad luck or an unfortunate situation.

examples.everyday: You can't make it to the barbecue? That's a shame, we'll miss you.
examples.professional: The vendor withdrew from the bid, which is a shame given the quality of their earlier work.
examples.analytical: It is a shame that public debate so often collapses into labels rather than arguments that can be tested.

nuance.analogy: Like a small pebble in your shoe: not a disaster, but it stings enough to notice.
nuance.etymology: From Old English scamu, 'shame' or 'disgrace'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun 'shame' with the adjective 'ashamed'; 'that's a shame' is about bad luck, not guilt.
Saying the word with a short vowel like 'sham'; the vowel is a long ay.

senses.definition: Attempted remediation of a health problem following a diagnosis, usually synonymous with treatment.
senses.example: inclined bed therapy

senses.definition: Specifically, psychotherapy.
senses.example: After her divorce, she started therapy with a counselor who specialized in anxiety.

senses.definition: (Can we add an example for this sense?) Healing power or quality.
senses.example: Gardening offered a quiet therapy that helped her heal after the long winter.

senses.definition: (rare) To treat with a therapy.
senses.example: The team decided to therapy the injury with heat and ultrasound.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) To undergo a therapy.
senses.example: She had to therapy three times a week after the accident.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Treatment to help heal or improve a physical or mental health problem, often through regular sessions with a trained professional.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The 'ther' is pronounced like 'thair', and the 'a' in the middle reduces to a quick 'uh'. Keep the final 'ee' clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Attitudes have become much more open, so talking about being in therapy is usually accepted without embarrassment.
nuance.usage_note: In American conversation 'therapy' usually means talk therapy or psychotherapy, so saying 'I go to therapy' is normal and not private. 'Physical therapy' (often called PT) is for injuries and mobility. Casually, 'retail therapy' means shopping to feel better, which is a joke, not medical advice. As a verb, 'therapy' is rare, so use 'treat' or 'be in therapy' instead.

distinctions.note: Treatment is broader and can mean any medical care, while therapy usually refers to an ongoing process such as talk or physical rehabilitation.
Counseling is usually short-term support or advice, while therapy may be longer and deeper.
Medication means drugs, while therapy refers to non-drug sessions or exercises, although the two are often combined.

examples.everyday: I've been going to therapy since spring, and it has really helped me sleep better.
examples.professional: Our employee wellness program covers up to twelve therapy sessions per year.
examples.analytical: Freud's clinical method helped launch the modern idea of therapy as a talking cure, a claim that psychologists still debate.

nuance.analogy: Therapy is like a personal trainer for the mind: regular practice builds strength you can use on your own.
nuance.etymology: From Greek therapeia meaning medical treatment or service, from therapeuein meaning to attend, serve or heal.
common_mistakes: Mixing up therapy (the treatment) with therapist (the person): say 'I see my therapist,' not 'I see my therapy.'
Saying 'make therapy' instead of 'go to therapy' or 'do therapy.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word therapeia, meaning healing or care, appears in the New Testament. Luke 9:11 describes Jesus welcoming crowds and healing those who needed healing, and Revelation 22:2 speaks of the leaves of the tree of life being for the healing of the nations. These passages use the word for restoration, not for psychological treatment.

therapy.etymology: From New Latin *therapīa*, from Ancient Greek *θεραπεία* (“service, medical treatment”), from *θεραπεύω* (“to serve, treat medically”) *-ία*.

senses.definition: To fully consider, so as to understand all the consequences of.

core.definition: To consider all the details and possible consequences of something before acting on it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THROO, and the 'th' in 'through' is voiceless and should be a soft, light sound. The 'r' in 'through' is pronounced as the 'thr' cluster, so say the 'thr' together rather than adding a vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It signals careful, responsible planning and is valued in professional and personal decisions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'think through' when they want someone to plan carefully, as in 'Did you think through the risks?' It appears often in workplace reviews, project planning and family conversations about big decisions. A natural reply is 'Yes, I've thought it through, and here's my plan.'

distinctions.note: 'Think through' stresses analyzing all consequences and steps, while 'think over' focuses more on reflecting before deciding.
To analyze is a formal, technical term for breaking something into parts; 'think through' is a conversational phrase for planning practically.

examples.everyday: Before you quit your job to start a business, you should really think through how you'll pay the bills.
examples.professional: Before we launch the new feature, let's think through the rollback plan and the edge cases with the engineering team.
examples.analytical: A careful ethicist must think through the implications of a principle before applying it to hard cases.

nuance.analogy: Like walking a route on a map in your head before driving it, so you see every turn in advance.
nuance.etymology: From 'think' plus 'through', from Old English thurh, meaning to go across or completely to the end.
common_mistakes: Using 'think through' to mean 'think about' casually, when it implies detailed, complete consideration.
Mispronouncing 'through' as 'thru-oo' or adding a vowel between 'th' and 'r'.

conversation.text: Did you think this through before you quit your job?
Let's think through what could go wrong.

senses.definition: Having thorns or spines.
senses.example: The hikers pushed through a thorny thicket of blackberry bushes that scratched their arms.

senses.definition: Troublesome or vexatious.
senses.example: thorny issues

senses.definition: Aloof and irritable.
senses.example: My boss has been thorny all week, snapping at everyone over trivial mistakes in the reports.

core.definition: Full of thorns; or, of a problem or question, difficult and sensitive, hard to handle without causing trouble.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, THOR-nee, with a rhotic 'or' and a long 'ee' at the end. Do not add an extra syllable such as 'THOR-un-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing issues; neutral when describing plants.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for a difficult issue that needs careful handling, especially in politics, business and meetings, where it sounds measured and polite. For a difficult person, 'prickly' is more natural. In casual talk you might say 'tricky' or 'messy' instead.

distinctions.note: Tricky is casual and suggests something needs cleverness; thorny emphasizes sensitivity or contention.
Prickly describes a sharp surface or an irritable person; thorny describes a troublesome issue.
Knotty suggests a complex intellectual puzzle; thorny suggests a problem that is uncomfortable to deal with.

examples.everyday: Figuring out who pays for the new fence is a thorny question with my brother.
examples.professional: Data retention across regions is a thorny issue that legal needs to weigh in on before we launch.
examples.analytical: Whether divine foreknowledge is compatible with human freedom remains a thorny question in philosophical theology.

nuance.analogy: Like a rosebush: beautiful from a distance, but you need to be careful how you grab it.
nuance.etymology: From thorn (Old English þorn) plus the suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using 'thorny' for a shy person; 'prickly' is more natural for people
Pronouncing the first vowel as a long 'o', as in 'thoh-nee'
nuance.biblical_note: Genesis 3:18 describes the ground cursed after the Fall so that it brings forth 'thorns and thistles' for humans to labor against. In Matthew 13:7 seed falls among thorns that grow up and choke it, and Matthew 13:22 explains that the cares of the world and the delight in riches choke the word. The thorny ground in this parable stands for hearts crowded by worldly concerns.

thorny.etymology: From Middle English *thorny*, *þorny*, *þorni*, from Old English *þorniġ*, from **þornag*.

senses.definition: To cause something one is holding to drop, often forcefully.
senses.example: The soldiers threw down their weapons and surrendered.

senses.definition: To produce or perform (something) admirably or forcefully.
senses.example: The rookie threw down a career-high twenty points in her first playoff game.

senses.definition: To accomplish or produce something in a grand, respectable, or successful manner; to "represent".
senses.example: Our team really threw down at the regional competition and made the whole town proud.

senses.definition: To drink a large amount quickly.
senses.example: "We need to finish these five pitchers in half an hour, so throw down as fast as you can!"

senses.definition: To fight; to make a stand.
senses.example: When the gang challenged them, the outnumbered crew decided to throw down in the parking lot.

senses.definition: To make an individual contribution to a group effort (e.g. money pool, collaborative record album).
senses.example: "We're goin' in on a pizza; you in?" "Yeah, I'll throw down."

senses.definition: (dated) To destroy or demolish.
senses.example: to throw down a tower
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To drop or put something down forcefully or abruptly; in informal use, to perform something impressively.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on down, while throw is lighter. In fluent speech the words link smoothly as 'throh-DOWN,' and the w in down is silent in the sound of the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when literal; the informal performance sense is positive, and the 'throw down' meaning to fight is aggressive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'throw down' literally, as in 'throw down your bag,' or informally to praise a performance, as in 'she threw down a great set.' In some circles it can mean to fight, though 'throw hands' is more common. A natural reply is 'Nice!' or 'That sounds great.'

distinctions.note: Drop is simple and neutral; throw down adds force or abruptness.
Throw out means discard; throw down means put something down forcefully, with no sense of getting rid of it.

examples.everyday: He threw down his keys on the counter and said he'd had a long day.
examples.professional: She threw down a great presentation on the new dashboard, and the VP asked for a repeat.
examples.analytical: The lecture threw down a rigorous defense of the argument, leaving few objections standing.

nuance.analogy: Like setting a heavy bag on the floor with a thud: the motion is sudden and forceful.
nuance.etymology: From throw and down; the figurative senses developed from the literal meaning.
common_mistakes: Placing a pronoun after the verb incorrectly; say 'throw it down,' not 'throw down it.'
Assuming the informal 'perform well' sense is formal; it is slang.

senses.definition: A storm consisting of thunder and lightning produced by a cumulonimbus, usually accompanied with heavy rain, wind, and sometimes hail; and in rarer cases sleet, freezing rain, or snow.

core.definition: A storm with lightning and thunder, usually with heavy rain and sometimes hail or strong wind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on THUN. The second syllable is a reduced American 'der,' so do not pronounce a full 'duh' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It is a neutral weather term, but it often signals danger or disruption.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thunderstorm in weather forecasts, everyday talk and safety warnings. People say 'there's a thunderstorm coming' or 'a severe thunderstorm warning' with no formality. A natural reply to news of one is 'Good thing we're inside.'

distinctions.note: Storm is the general term for strong weather, while thunderstorm specifically means one with thunder and lightning.
A hurricane is a large tropical cyclone with sustained winds of at least 74 miles per hour, much more powerful than a usual thunderstorm.

examples.everyday: Let's stay in tonight because there's a thunderstorm coming.
examples.professional: The outdoor event has been moved indoors because the forecast calls for thunderstorms after noon.
examples.analytical: The meteorological model distinguishes ordinary rain from a thunderstorm by the presence of lightning and cumulonimbus clouds.

nuance.analogy: A thunderstorm is nature's loud reminder that the sky can change in minutes.
nuance.etymology: From thunder, from Old English thunor, plus storm, from Old English storm.
common_mistakes: Using thunderstorm for any rainy weather, when it requires lightning and thunder.
Pronouncing the word with equal stress on both parts.

conversation.text: There's a thunderstorm coming, so get out of the pool.
We had a big thunderstorm last night, and the power went out.
Afternoon thunderstorms are common in Florida in the summer.

senses.definition: The action of making tired. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The steady tiring of the crew during the long shift slowed production noticeably.

senses.definition: Bits of bone and tough organic material from a corpse given to hawks to abate their hunger.
senses.example: The falconer tossed a handful of tiring to the hawk after its hunt.

senses.definition: That tires or tire.
senses.example: Carrying my bags up four flights of stairs is very tiring.

core.definition: Making you feel tired or exhausted, especially because of physical or mental effort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the word has two syllables, not three. The middle is a quick American r-sound, so do not add an extra vowel between 'tire' and '-ing'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes an activity that drains energy, often without implying that the activity is bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tiring' to describe a long trip, a hard day or a demanding job, as in 'It was a tiring day at the hospital.' The noun sense, meaning the act of making someone tired, is rare and mostly appears in older or technical writing. In everyday speech, use the adjective.

distinctions.note: Tired describes how a person feels; tiring describes what causes the feeling.
Tiring is about physical or mental exhaustion, while tiresome is about irritation or boredom.

examples.everyday: The drive from Denver was long and tiring, so we're staying home tonight.
examples.professional: Running two incident calls back to back is tiring, so let's rotate on-call shifts next month.
examples.analytical: Theologians have long noted that spiritual discipline can be tiring, yet it is also a source of renewal.

nuance.analogy: A tiring day is like a phone battery that drops quickly when you run many apps at once.
nuance.etymology: From tire, the verb, plus the suffix -ing; tire comes from Old English tȳrian, to weary.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I'm tiring' when you mean 'I'm tired'; 'tiring' describes the thing that causes the feeling.
Pronouncing it with an extra syllable, as 'TYE-ur-ree-ing'.

core.definition: Paul's Gentile companion and co-worker, to whom the Epistle to Titus is addressed; he led the church on Crete.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced, unstressed 'tus', so do not give it a full 'toos' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; as a given name it is common in the United States and carries no special tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American English Titus is a personal name and also the name of a book of the Bible, which RSV names Titus and abbreviates Tit. Americans in church settings will refer to the letter by the book name, such as 'We're studying Titus this month.' Used as a first name, it is a normal American name.

distinctions.note: Timothy is another co-worker of Paul, and two letters are addressed to him, while Titus receives one letter addressed to him alone.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's son is named Titus, and he's a great kid.
examples.professional: Our Bible study curriculum moves from Timothy to Titus this month.
examples.analytical: The Epistle to Titus presents Titus as a delegate who must appoint elders on Crete and correct false teaching.

nuance.analogy: Titus is like a trusted deputy whom a senior leader sends to finish difficult work in a distant place.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Titos, a name of uncertain meaning, borrowed into Latin as Titus.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'ti-TUS'.
Confusing Titus with Timothy, the other co-worker of Paul.
nuance.biblical_note: Titus was a Gentile Greek companion of Paul, and Galatians 2:1-3 notes that he was not compelled to be circumcised when he went up to Jerusalem with Paul and Barnabas. 2 Corinthians 7:6-7 describes Titus bringing Paul comfort and a report from the church at Corinth. Titus 1:4-5 introduces him as Paul's true child in the faith and says Paul left him on Crete to set right what was defective and appoint elders in every town.

senses.definition: A small secondary lavatory having a fixture used for urination and defecation and sink but no bathtub or shower.
senses.example: The new house has a half bath with a toilet and sink downstairs.

senses.definition: A fixture used for urination and defecation, particularly one with a large bowl and ring-shaped seat which uses water to flush the waste material into a septic tank or sewer system.
senses.example: My toilet got clogged. Now the bathroom's flooded.

senses.definition: A very shabby or dirty place.
senses.example: That motel room was a filthy toilet, and we left before sunrise.

senses.definition: A woman.
senses.example: Who's that old toilet giving Frank the eye at the bar?

senses.definition: To use (urinate or defecate in) a toilet.
senses.example: Before the long drive, Dad made sure we all toileted at the rest stop.

senses.definition: To assist another (a child, etc.) in using a toilet.
senses.example: Our nurse taught the twins to toilet independently before they started preschool.

senses.definition: (dated) To dress and groom oneself.
senses.example: Give me an hour to toilet, and then we can head to the dance.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A bathroom fixture, usually a bowl with a seat, used for urinating and defecating and flushed with water; also the room that contains it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, TOY. The second syllable is a reduced 'lit', with a short, weak vowel, so it does not sound like 'toy-LET'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in everyday use, though a bit blunt in polite conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say bathroom for the room in a home, and restroom for a public room, especially in a restaurant or office. Asking for the toilet can sound blunt in polite company. Casual speech may use the john. Outside the US, the British say loo, but Americans do not use that word for a toilet.

distinctions.note: Bathroom is the polite, everyday word for the room with a toilet, sink and often a shower or tub.
Restroom is the polite public word for a room with toilets, often in a store, restaurant or office.
John is informal American slang for a toilet or bathroom and sounds casual.

examples.everyday: Could you plunge the toilet? It's totally clogged and the bathroom is flooding.
examples.professional: The facilities team is replacing every toilet in the east wing this month to save water.
examples.analytical: In public health, toilets are central to sanitation, because keeping waste away from drinking water sharply reduces disease.

nuance.analogy: Like a sealed drain built for the body's waste: a flush sends away what the body no longer needs.
nuance.etymology: From French toilette, a diminutive of toile, cloth, originally a cloth covering used at a dressing table.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'toy-LET' with stress on the second syllable.
Asking for the toilet in polite company, where Americans say bathroom or restroom.
Using the British word loo, which Americans do not normally say.

toilet.etymology: From Middle French *toilette*, diminutive of *toile* (“cloth”), from their use to protect clothing while shaving or arranging hair.

conversation.text: The toilet keeps running after you flush it.
Don't flush paper towels down the toilet.
The toilet in the upstairs bathroom is broken, so use the one downstairs.

senses.definition: Clothing that is too big.

core.definition: Describing clothing that is too big or baggy and does not fit the body closely.

pronunciation.tip: Loose rhymes with goose, with a long oo sound, not with 'lose' as in 'lose your keys'. The stress is on the second word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a fit problem and is usually a practical remark when shopping or dressing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'too loose' for clothing that hangs off the body, especially in shopping or fitting situations. For clothing that is too big overall, people also say 'too big'. A natural reply might be 'Yeah, the waist is too loose, so I'll try a smaller size'.

distinctions.note: Too big is the general term for a size problem, while too loose focuses on how the fabric hangs or fits the body.
Baggy describes a deliberately loose style, while too loose describes a fit that is not what the person wanted.

examples.everyday: These jeans are too loose at the waist, so I'm going to get a smaller pair.
examples.professional: Our uniform shirts run too loose in the shoulders, so the size chart needs updating.
examples.analytical: A tailor's measurements show the garment is too loose, which explains why the costume lacks the period's structure.

nuance.analogy: Too loose is like a rope that has been pulled too far apart: it does not hold the shape it should.
common_mistakes: Saying 'lose' for 'loose', which changes the meaning and pronunciation.
Using 'loose' to mean 'free' when talking about a size problem.

conversation.text: This shirt is too loose on me. I need a small.
The belt helps, because these pants are a little too loose.
If the ring is too loose, the jeweler can resize it.

senses.definition: The ability to remember in great detail; possessing photographic memory.

core.definition: The ability to remember almost everything in vivid detail, as if you had a nearly perfect memory.

pronunciation.tip: In the noun recall, the main stress falls on RE, while the verb stresses the second syllable (ree-KAWL). Americans often drop the vowel before the l in total.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises someone's excellent memory, though it is hyperbole.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use total recall casually to praise someone with an excellent memory, often about sports stats, song lyrics or names. It is an exaggeration, not a medical claim, so do not use it literally about a serious memory condition. The phrase is also the title of a 1990 science fiction film starring Arnold Schwarzenegger, so people may joke about it.

distinctions.note: Photographic memory describes a claimed ability to see a page in your mind; total recall is broader praise and less technical.
Good memory is a neutral description; total recall is hyperbolic and emphatic.

examples.everyday: My grandpa has total recall for every baseball game he has ever watched.
examples.professional: She has total recall of every API change, so she always knows what broke.
examples.analytical: Claims of total recall, like those sometimes attributed to savants, rarely survive careful testing and controlled comparison.

nuance.analogy: A library where every book is always in the right place and nothing is ever misfiled.
nuance.etymology: Total from Late Latin totalis; recall from Latin recallare, to call back.
common_mistakes: Saying total memory in English, which is not the usual idiom.
Stressing the second syllable of the noun recall; in the noun it is REE-kawl.

senses.definition: To make totalitarian.

core.definition: To turn a country, group or institution into a totalitarian system that controls nearly every part of public and private life.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TAIR, and the -ize ending carries secondary stress. Say the -ian part lightly, almost as ee-uhn.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies sweeping and oppressive control.
nuance.usage_note: This rare verb appears mostly in political writing and history about the twentieth century. Americans more often say turn into a totalitarian state, or use the noun totalitarianism. Using it in casual talk would sound stiff or like a lecture, and because it is strongly critical, use it carefully when describing real governments.

distinctions.note: Authoritarian rule concentrates power but may leave private life alone; totalitarian rule seeks control of nearly all social and private life.
Totalize means to make total or add up; it is not political, so do not use it for government control.

examples.everyday: My uncle worries the new rules could totalitarianize the workplace, though I think that is an exaggeration.
examples.professional: Critics warned that the reorganization would totalitarianize internal communications by monitoring every message.
examples.analytical: Some historians argue that terror is what allows a regime to totalitarianize every social institution, not merely to govern it.

nuance.analogy: Like a house where one person controls every room, lock and window, and no door opens without permission.
nuance.etymology: Totalitarian was coined in the 1920s from Italian totalitario; the suffix -ize was added in English.
common_mistakes: Using totalitarianize casually for any strict rule; it implies total control of society.
Confusing it with authoritarianize-type meanings; the key difference is the breadth of control.

senses.definition: The territory of a town.
senses.example: The township's boundaries were redrawn after the new highway split the old farmland in two.

senses.definition: A subdivision of a county.
senses.example: Our county has nine townships, and each one elects its own trustees to manage local roads.

senses.definition: A small town.
senses.example: My grandparents raised five kids in a quiet township of about four hundred people.

core.definition: In many US states, a local government unit smaller than a county, with its own elected officials, roads and services.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TOWN; the final syllable is a short 'ship' with a reduced vowel, not 'sheep'. The sh is a single sound, so do not add a t or an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; an administrative term rather than an emotional one.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use township for local government units in states such as Pennsylvania, Michigan, Ohio and New Jersey, where it may handle zoning, road maintenance and police. Many residents call their place a town in casual talk, even when it is legally a township. Use the formal name on forms and addresses.

distinctions.note: Town is a general term for a community, while township is a specific legal unit with defined borders and powers in certain states.
A county is larger and contains townships in states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Ohio.
A borough is another type of municipality in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, usually more compact and urban than a township.

examples.everyday: I just got a notice from the township saying trash pickup changes next month.
examples.professional: The township engineer confirmed that the new road will meet the state's drainage standards.
examples.analytical: The township, as a unit of local government, illustrates how American federalism distributes power across many layers below the state.

nuance.analogy: A township is a local layer of government between your neighborhood and the county, handling everyday services.
nuance.etymology: From town and -ship, from Old English -scipe, meaning state or district.
common_mistakes: Assuming every township is a town or city; in some states it is a rural governmental area.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'sheep' rather than the short 'ship' sound.

township.etymology: From Middle English *towneship*, *townschip*, *tounshipe*, *tunscipe*, from Old English *tūnsċipe* (“the inhabitants of a town; township”), equivalent to *town* + *-ship*.

senses.definition: To convert a representation of language, typically speech but also sign language, etc. to a written representation of it. The term now usually implies the conversion of speech to text by a human transcriptionist with the assistance of a computer for word processing and sometimes also for speech recognition, the process of a computer interpreting speech and converting it to text.
senses.example: The nurse transcribed the doctor's dictated notes into a written report before lunch.

senses.definition: To make such a conversion from live or recorded speech to text.
senses.example: The doctor made several recordings today which she will transcribe into medical reports tomorrow.

senses.definition: To transfer data from one recording medium to another.
senses.example: I transcribed the old VHS tapes onto a hard drive so the family could keep them.

senses.definition: To cause DNA to undergo transcription.
senses.example: Researchers found that the gene is transcribed only when the cell receives a specific signal.

senses.definition: To represent speech by phonetic symbols.
senses.example: In the linguistics seminar, we transcribed each vowel using the International Phonetic Alphabet.

senses.definition: To adapt a composition for a voice or instrument other than the original; to notate live or recorded music.
senses.example: The arranger transcribed the piano sonata for full orchestra, keeping the original harmonies intact.

core.definition: To write out spoken words in written form, or to convert an audio recording into text, or to write music in a different notation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SKRYBE, and the first syllable is a short 'a'. Learners often stress the first syllable, which sounds like the wrong word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical task.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transcribe for converting recorded interviews, meetings or voicemails into text, often with the help of software. In general conversation, people say type up or write down. The word is common in offices, courts, journalism and research.

distinctions.note: Transcribe means to write the same language in a different form, while translate means to change the language into another one.
Record means to capture sound or video. Transcribe means to turn that recording into written text.

examples.everyday: Could you transcribe that voicemail for me so I can read it?
examples.professional: I will transcribe the customer interviews and send you the cleaned text by Friday.
examples.analytical: Linguists transcribe speech with the International Phonetic Alphabet to capture sounds that ordinary spelling misses.

nuance.analogy: To transcribe is like copying a letter from a dictated tape: the meaning stays the same, but it moves from sound to paper.
nuance.etymology: From Latin transcribere, 'to copy over', from trans- 'across' and scribere 'to write'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (TRAN-scribe) instead of the second.
Using transcribe to mean translate.
Pronouncing the final -e as a separate syllable.

transcribe.etymology: Latin *trānscrībō* (“to write again in another place, transcribe, copy”).

senses.definition: A person who is transferred.
A person to whom title or ownership is conveyed.

core.definition: A person who is moved or reassigned to another job, school or location, or to whom property or legal title is passed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, EE, so the word ends with a long 'ee' sound. The first syllables are quick and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a person in a formal process such as a school transfer, a company relocation or a legal conveyance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transferee mostly in formal settings: a company moves a transferee to another office, or a university admits a transferee student. In casual talk they'd say the person who transferred or someone moving to our branch. A transferee is the person being moved, not the one doing the moving.

distinctions.note: A transferee receives the transfer, while a transferor gives or conveys it.
Transfer student is the everyday term for a student moving between colleges; transferee is more formal and used in administrative or legal contexts.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's son is a transferee at the local college, so he's still getting used to campus.
examples.professional: Our HR team will schedule an orientation for the transferee before she starts in the Denver office.
examples.analytical: In property law, the transferee's rights depend on the transferor's title, which is why due diligence matters.

nuance.analogy: Like a package: the sender is the transferor, and the person it arrives at is the transferee.
nuance.etymology: From transfer plus the suffix -ee, meaning the person who receives or is affected by the action.
common_mistakes: Swapping transferee and transferor, which reverses their roles.
Using transferee for every person who changes jobs; the word fits a formal or assigned move.

senses.definition: Any injury to the body of a living thing.
senses.example: mild trauma; major trauma

senses.definition: Serious injury, resulting from predation, violence, an accident such as a fall, a vehicle crash, etc.
senses.example: We're not talking about paper cuts or sprains here — we're talking about trauma.

senses.definition: An emotional wound leading to psychological injury.
senses.example: What these patients eventually realized was that they all had trauma that had fed into their addictions.

senses.definition: An event that causes great distress.
senses.example: The earthquake here 14 years ago was a national trauma that still affects the economy today.

core.definition: A deeply distressing experience that causes lasting emotional harm, or a serious physical injury.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Americans often use the vowel of 'caught' here, and some say TROW-muh; the final syllable is a reduced 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; describes serious harm, and can be overused in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trauma for both medical injuries and deep emotional wounds, but in casual talk they often say it was traumatic for a stressful event that was less serious. Saying someone has trauma is a clinical or therapeutic framing, so use it carefully. Friends usually ask are you okay or that must have been hard rather than naming trauma directly.

distinctions.note: Stress is ordinary pressure that usually passes, while trauma is severe enough to cause lasting psychological harm.
Injury is any damage to the body, while in emotional use trauma refers to psychological harm, though it can also mean physical injury.

examples.everyday: Watching the house burn down was a real trauma for my mom, and she still gets nervous near fires.
examples.professional: Our HR team is trained to respond when an employee has experienced trauma on the job, such as a serious accident.
examples.analytical: Trauma does not simply cause fear; it can break the story through which a person understands their own life.

nuance.analogy: Trauma is like a bone fracture that heals crooked: the wound closes, but the structure keeps shaping how you move.
nuance.etymology: From Greek trauma, 'wound'.
common_mistakes: Using trauma for a minor stressful event, which can sound exaggerated
Saying I am very trauma instead of I am traumatized or it was traumatic

senses.definition: Like or in the way of treason.
senses.example: His treasonous actions earned Benedict Arnold eternal scorn.

core.definition: Involving or resembling treason, which is the betrayal of one's country or government, often by helping its enemies.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllables reduce to 'zuh-nus'. Do not confuse the spelling with 'treasure', which is pronounced differently.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It accuses someone of disloyalty to a country or a cause.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use treasonous most often in political debate and news coverage, where it can be an accusation, as in 'The senator called the leak treasonous.' The legal crime of treason under the U.S. Constitution is narrow, so careful speakers may prefer treasonable in legal contexts. Using the word loosely in casual talk can sound heated or dramatic.

distinctions.note: Treasonable is more often used in legal and constitutional discussions, while treasonous is more common in political rhetoric.
Traitorous is broader and applies to personal betrayal of friends, family, or trust, while treasonous specifically concerns a country or government.

examples.everyday: My uncle called the senator's comments treasonous, and we argued about it all through dinner.
examples.professional: A leaked customer list is not treasonous, but it is a serious breach of our data policy and needs review.
examples.analytical: Whether leaking classified information is treasonous depends on intent and on the statute, not only on the harm done.

nuance.analogy: Treasonous conduct is like cutting the rope of a climbing partner: it betrays the people whose trust holds you up.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English tresoun, from Old French traison, from Latin traditio, 'a handing over'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the spelling and sound with 'treasure', which has a different vowel pattern.
Saying 'treasonus' instead of 'treasonous', with the ending -us as in 'famous'.

senses.definition: To reduce slightly; to cut; especially, to remove excess.
senses.example: He trimmed his beard before the interview.

senses.definition: To decorate or adorn; especially of a Christmas tree.
senses.example: They traditionally trim the tree on Christmas Eve.

senses.definition: To adjust the positions of control surfaces, sometimes using trim tabs, so as to modify or eliminate the aircraft's tendency to pitch, roll, or yaw when the cockpit controls are released.
senses.example: The pilot trimmed the plane so it would hold altitude without her touching the yoke.

senses.definition: To make trim; to put in due order for any purpose; to make right, neat, or pleasing; to adjust.
senses.example: Before the photo shoot, she trimmed the hedges and straightened the garden path.

senses.definition: To dress; to make smooth.
senses.example: The carpenter trimmed the rough edges of the door so it closed smoothly.

senses.definition: To change the carbon rods of (an arc lamp).
senses.example: The projectionist trimmed the carbon rods of the old arc lamp before each show.

senses.definition: To modify the angle relative to the water by shifting cargo or ballast; to adjust for sailing; to assume, or cause to assume a certain position, or trim, in the water.
senses.example: We trimmed the boat by moving the heavy cooler to the stern before the squall.

senses.definition: To modify the angle (of the sails) relative to the wind, especially to set them at the most advantageous angle.
senses.example: Dad trimmed the mainsail as the wind shifted, and the boat picked up speed.

senses.definition: (dated) To balance; to fluctuate between parties, so as to appear to favor each.
senses.example: For years the senator trimmed between the two parties, never committing to either.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To rebuke; to reprove.
senses.example: Aunt Ruth trimmed him soundly for lying about the broken vase.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To beat or thrash.
senses.example: The bully trimmed the smaller boy behind the gym, and everyone pretended not to see.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (historical) To cut back the wick of (a lamp) to maintain a clean, bright flame.
senses.example: Every evening my great-grandmother trimmed the lamp so it would burn clean and bright.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Decoration; especially, decoration placed along edges or borders.
senses.example: Paint the house white with blue trim.

senses.definition: A haircut, especially a moderate one to touch up an existing style.
senses.example: I went to the hairdresser for a trim but came back nearly bald.

senses.definition: Dress; gear; ornaments.
senses.example: The shop sold holiday trim, ribbons, tinsel, and glass ornaments.

senses.definition: The manner in which something is equipped or adorned; order; disposition.
senses.example: to be in good trim

senses.definition: Features optionally available on a vehicle; an established configuration of such features within a model (a trim level).
senses.example: This model of car comes in three different trims.

senses.definition: The state of adjustment of control surfaces such that the desired attitude can be maintained without requiring the continuous application of force to the cockpit controls.
senses.example: The plane flies hands-off once the trim is set correctly for cruise altitude.

senses.definition: The mechanism(s) used to trim an aircraft in roll, pitch, and/or yaw.
senses.example: The trim on the rudder failed, so the pilot had to fly with constant pressure.

senses.definition: The female genitalia.
Sexual intercourse with a woman.
The horizontal position of an underwater diver.
senses.example: Keep your trim level in the water, with your body flat and your fins pointing back.

senses.definition: The fore-and-aft angle of the vessel to the water, with reference to the cargo and ballast; the manner in which a vessel floats on the water, whether on an even keel or down by the head or stern.
The arrangement of the sails with reference to the wind.
Any of the three cut edges of book pages, trimmed with a shear after binding.
Physically fit.
senses.example: He goes jogging every day to keep in trim.

senses.definition: Slender, lean.
senses.example: a trim figure

senses.definition: Neat or smart in appearance.
senses.example: a trim lawn

senses.definition: In good order; properly managed or maintained.
With sails well trimmed.

core.definition: To cut off small amounts of something to make it neater, smaller, or more even, or to reduce costs.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short, the same as in him, and the final m is a clear closed lip sound. Make sure the r is pronounced clearly, as American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive when it means tidying up, or negative when it means cutting budgets or staff, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trim for everyday grooming, such as trimming a beard or hedges, and for business budgets, as in trim the budget or trim staff. Trim the fat is a common phrase for removing unnecessary costs. In the workplace, trim can sound like a cut in people or money, so listen to context.

distinctions.note: Cut is the general word for dividing or removing material. Trim implies removing a small or excess part to improve the shape.
Prune usually refers to plants, removing branches to promote health or growth. Trim can apply to hair, hedges, edges, or budgets.

examples.everyday: Can you trim the hedges along the driveway before the neighbors come over this weekend?
examples.professional: Management wants to trim the marketing budget by ten percent before the next quarter begins.
examples.analytical: The argument trims away the dogmatic claims, leaving only the testable core of the hypothesis.

nuance.analogy: Trimming is like editing a draft: you remove what is extra so the important shape becomes clear.
nuance.etymology: From Old English trymman, meaning to make firm or strong, later meaning to put in order.
common_mistakes: Using trim for cutting large or whole objects, where cut or chop is more natural.
Saying trim the costs of the bills when the standard phrase is trim costs or trim the budget.

trim.etymology: From Middle English *trimen*, *trymen*, *trumen*, from Old English *trymman* (“to make firm; strengthen”), from **trummjan*, from Proto-Germanic **trumjaną* (“to make fast; strengthen”), from Proto-Germanic **trumaz* (“firm; strong; sound”).

senses.definition: Something that twirls.
Someone who twirls something.
A majorette who twirls a baton.
A pitcher.
senses.example: The twirler threw a fastball that struck out the side in the ninth inning.

core.definition: A person who twirls a baton, especially a majorette in a marching band or parade.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable; the final -er is an unstressed reduced vowel, not 'air'. Make the r in the middle silent-sounding but keep the vowel rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; often associated with school sports bands and parades.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, twirler is most often used for a baton twirler in a high school or college marching band or a parade. Americans also say majorette for the same role, though majorette is more old-fashioned. The word is a friendly, everyday term when talking about school or local events.

distinctions.note: Majorette is an older, more traditional term for a baton leader in a band; twirler is the more general and current word.
A drum major leads the band with a baton or gestures, while a twirler performs tricks with a baton.

examples.everyday: My daughter is a baton twirler, and she practices every Saturday morning at the high school.
examples.professional: The marching band needs two more twirlers for the halftime show next month.
examples.analytical: The role of the twirler in American parade culture combines athletic display with the ceremonial visibility of the band.

nuance.analogy: A twirler is like a juggler whose only prop is a baton, spinning it in a steady rhythm.
nuance.etymology: Formed from twirl with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun twirler with the verb twirl when a noun is needed.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'ler' with a full vowel instead of a reduced one.

senses.definition: Having two legs or feet.
senses.example: The biologist studied the two-footed gait of early hominids in the fossil record.

senses.definition: Using both feet.
Ambidextrous of the feet; having equal ability with either foot.
senses.example: The soccer coach praised his two-footed striker, who could shoot equally well with either foot.

core.definition: Able to use both feet equally well; in soccer, a dangerous tackle made with both feet off the ground.

pronunciation.tip: Stress usually falls on TWO. The vowel in foot is the short oo of book, not the long oo of food, and the word ends in a short -id.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general use; negative when describing a reckless tackle.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech two-footed mostly appears in sports talk, especially soccer, where a two-footed tackle is a dangerous foul, and in coaching praise for a player who can use both feet well. For a player who is equally good with both feet, Americans may also say the player is good with either foot. Calling someone two-footed is usually a compliment, unless you are describing a reckless challenge.

distinctions.note: Used for hands or for equal skill in general; two-footed is specific to feet, often in sports.
Describe a preferred foot; two-footed means equal ability with either foot.
Means having two legs; two-footed means using both feet with skill.

examples.everyday: My son is two-footed, so he can kick the ball with either foot during pickup games.
examples.professional: The coach wants a two-footed winger, because defenders then cannot predict which foot he will shoot with.
examples.analytical: Commentators treat a two-footed tackle as reckless, since it puts both feet off the ground and endangers the opponent's leg.

nuance.analogy: Like a pianist who plays equally well with both hands, the player moves the ball with either foot.
nuance.etymology: From two and footed, meaning having feet.
common_mistakes: Assuming it refers to a foot problem or disability.
Pronouncing foot like food, with a long oo vowel.

senses.definition: Having no additional decoration or embellishment; plain and simple.

core.definition: Plain and simple, without added decoration, ornament or embellishment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -DORN-, which is a strong 'or' vowel with the r pronounced. The un- and a- syllables are light, and the word ends in a single d sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive when praising simplicity and honesty; neutral or slightly negative when the result looks bare.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unadorned' to praise plain design, writing or speech, as in 'an unadorned truth.' It can also describe something that looks bare or unfinished. In everyday talk, people more often say 'plain' or 'simple,' while 'unadorned' sounds more polished or literary.

distinctions.note: 'Plain' is the general word for not fancy; 'unadorned' stresses specifically that nothing has been added.
'Austere' suggests severity or self-denial and can sound stern; 'unadorned' is more neutral and can sound elegant.

examples.everyday: I like our kitchen with its unadorned white walls and simple wooden table.
examples.professional: The slides were unadorned, with one chart per slide and no animation, which made the data easy to follow.
examples.analytical: Many Reformers preferred unadorned worship spaces, arguing that visual display could distract from the proclamation of the Word.

nuance.analogy: Like a plain wooden table before anyone adds a tablecloth or a vase: the structure is complete, and nothing extra is needed.
nuance.etymology: From adorn, from Latin adornare 'to equip, to decorate'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'UN-uh-dorned' instead of the stress on -DORN-.
Confusing 'unadorned' with 'adorable' because both come from the same Latin root but have very different meanings.
nuance.biblical_note: The idea of adornment appears in the New Testament. The Greek word kosmos, meaning both order and adornment, is used in passages that contrast outward decoration with inner character. 1 Peter 3:3-4 says a believer's beauty should lie in the hidden person of the heart rather than in braided hair and fine jewelry, and 1 Timothy 2:9-10 similarly urges modest dress and good works over costly display.

senses.definition: Not amused; thus often offended or put off.
