senses.example: The fisherman hauled his catch home in a wick slung over his shoulder.

senses.definition: Wickers collectively; also, synonym of wickerwork (“wickers woven together”).
senses.example: The gardener bought a load of wick to weave a new fence along the orchard.

senses.definition: Any piece of porous material that conveys liquid by capillary action; specifically, a strip of gauze placed in a wound, etc. to absorb fluids.
senses.example: The nurse packed a sterile wick into the wound to draw out the infected fluid.

senses.definition: Of a material (especially a textile): to convey or draw off (liquid) by capillary action.
senses.example: The fabric wicks perspiration away from the body.

senses.definition: Of a material: to convey or draw off liquid by capillary action.
senses.example: The cotton fabric wicks moisture away from the skin during long runs.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by through or up: of a liquid: to move by capillary action through a porous material.
senses.example: The moisture slowly wicked through the wood.

senses.definition: To strike (a stationary bowl or stone) with one's own bowl or stone just enough that the former changes direction; to cannon.
senses.example: He wicked the stationary stone just enough to nudge it toward the house.

senses.definition: To strike a stationary bowl or stone with one's own bowl or stone just enough that the former changes direction; to cannon.
senses.example: He wicked the stationary stone just enough to nudge it toward the house.

senses.definition: Synonym of quick (“alive, living; also, active, lively”).
senses.example: The preacher reminded us that Christ shall judge the wick and the dead.

core.definition: The cord or braid in a candle or oil lamp that draws up melted wax or fuel to burn with a flame.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable. Keep the vowel short, like the i in 'kit,' not a long 'ee.' Pronounce the w clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word for household objects, but the slang sense is crude and should be avoided in polite talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wick in everyday talk about candles, oil lamps, and camping, such as 'trim the wick.' Be careful: in informal slang, 'dip one's wick' is a crude expression for sexual activity, so avoid this phrase in polite company. The verb sense, to draw liquid by capillary action, is mostly technical, and the adjective 'quick' is archaic.

distinctions.note: A fuse is a device that burns to set off an explosion or spread fire. A wick is part of a candle or lamp that feeds fuel to a flame.
A candle is the whole object of wax and wick. The wick is only the central cord inside.

examples.everyday: Before you blow out the candle, trim the wick so it does not smoke.
examples.professional: Our product team tested several wick materials to see which burns the cleanest in the new candle line.
examples.analytical: In the parable image of Isaiah 42:3, the dimly burning wick stands for the faint hope the servant does not extinguish.

nuance.analogy: A wick is like a straw for fuel: it pulls the melted wax up to the flame, so the flame can keep burning.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wēoce (wick, lamp-wick), a word of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Using 'wick' for the flame itself, when it is the cord that carries fuel to the flame.
Using the slang sense ('dip one's wick') in polite conversation without knowing it is crude.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV translates Isaiah 42:3 as saying a dimly burning wick the servant will not quench. Matthew 12:20 quotes this verse to describe Jesus, who does not break a bruised reed or extinguish a smoldering wick. The image is of a small, weak flame that God refuses to snuff out.

wick.etymology: The is derived from Middle English *wek*, *weke*, *wicke* (“fibrous cord drawing fuel to flame of a candle, etc. material used to make this object”), from Old English *wēoce* (“wick”), from **weukā* (“flax bundle; wick”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European…

senses.definition: Having a large physical extent from side to side.
senses.example: We walked down a wide corridor.

senses.definition: Large in scope.
senses.example: The inquiry had a wide remit.

senses.definition: Overweight, obese.
senses.example: My grandfather grew wide in his later years, mostly from sitting in front of the television.

senses.definition: On one side or the other of the mark; too far sideways from the mark, the wicket, the batsman, etc.
senses.example: Two balls before lunch, he bowled a wide.

senses.definition: Of or supporting a greater range of text characters than can fit into the traditional 8-bit representation.
senses.example: a wide character; a wide stream

senses.definition: Operating at the side of the playing area.
senses.example: That team needs a decent wide player.

senses.definition: (dated) Made, as a vowel, with a less tense, and more open and relaxed, condition of the organs in the mouth.
senses.example: Our phonetics professor explained that the vowel in 'father' is wide, produced with the jaw dropped.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Extensively.
senses.example: He traveled far and wide.

senses.definition: Completely.
senses.example: He was wide awake.

senses.definition: Away from or to one side of a given goal.
senses.example: The arrow fell wide of the mark.

senses.definition: So as to leave or have a great space between the sides; so as to form a large opening.
senses.example: She opened the door wide so the movers could carry the sofa through.

senses.definition: A ball that passes so far from the batsman that the umpire deems it unplayable; the arm signal used by an umpire to signal a wide; the extra run added to the batting side's score.
senses.example: The bowler's delivery sailed well outside the leg stump, and the umpire's arm signaled a wide.

core.definition: Having a large distance from one side to the other. It is also used for a wide range of things, such as options, interests or groups.

pronunciation.tip: Use the diphthong of ride and side, with the final d voiced. Do not shorten it to a short i sound, and do not add an extra vowel at the end. The r-colored sounds do not apply here.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Wide describes size or extent without judgment, though its use for body size is informal and should be avoided.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wide constantly in everyday speech, for things like a wide street, a wide smile or a wide variety of options. Wide open and wide awake are also common in casual speech. The adjective meaning overweight is rare and can be insulting, so avoid it. The cricket sense of wide is mainly British and Commonwealth, and Americans would not use it in normal conversation.

distinctions.note: Broad is more formal and often used for shoulders, smiles or large general ideas, while wide is the everyday choice for measuring side-to-side distance.
Large describes overall size, while wide specifically describes the distance from one side to the other.

examples.everyday: The doorway is too narrow for the new couch, so we'll have to take off the legs to get it through.
examples.professional: We have a wide range of options for the Q3 launch, so let's narrow them down before the Thursday review.
examples.analytical: The study covers a wide range of outcomes, though its sample is narrow enough to limit what it can claim about the general population.

nuance.analogy: Wide is like the distance across a river: you measure it from one bank to the other.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wīd, meaning broad or extensive.
common_mistakes: Using wide to describe a person's body size, which can sound insulting.
Confusing wide with broad in casual speech, where wide is more natural for measurements.

wide.etymology: From Middle English *wid*, *wyd*, from Old English *wīd* (“wide, vast, broad, long; distant, far”), from Proto-Germanic **wīdaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **h₁weydʰh₁-* (“to divide, separate”), a dissimilated univerbation from **dwi-* + **dʰeh₁-*.

senses.definition: That benefits both or all parties, or that has two distinct benefits.
senses.example: win-win outcome

senses.definition: Ellipsis of win-win situation: A situation that benefits both or all parties, or that has two distinct benefits.
senses.example: They got their school project funded, and you got to look like a generous benefactor, plus some free advertising. It's a win-win.

core.definition: Beneficial to all sides, so that each party gains something from the outcome.

pronunciation.tip: The second word gets the main stress, so say win-WIN, not WIN-win. Both words have a short i as in 'sit'. Keep a clear pause between the two words.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests fairness and mutual benefit, and it is often used to end a debate happily.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use win-win very often in business, school, and family life: 'This schedule is a win-win.' It can be a noun or adjective. Some people find it a little buzzword-like, so in formal writing you might explain the benefit more concretely. In casual speech, 'everybody wins' is also natural.

distinctions.note: Zero-sum means one side's gain is exactly the other's loss; win-win means both sides can gain.
Compromise means each side gives something up; win-win means both sides actually gain.
Mutually beneficial is more formal and precise; win-win is more informal and common in American workplaces.

examples.everyday: Letting you take the car tonight and me take it tomorrow is a win-win for both of us.
examples.professional: Moving the release date to next quarter is a win-win: engineering gets time for testing and sales gets a stronger launch.
examples.analytical: Some economists argue that trade is a win-win arrangement only when both parties freely value what they receive more than what they give.

nuance.analogy: Like a two-lane bridge where traffic flows well in both directions at once.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first word: say win-WIN, not WIN-win.
Using it for a situation where only one side gains, which is a win-lose outcome.

conversation.text: Carpooling is a win-win: we save money and get time to chat.
The partnership is a win-win for both companies.
If you watch my dog and I water your plants, it's a win-win.
The new schedule is a win-win: the team gets flexibility and clients get faster replies.
Let's find a win-win solution that works for both departments.
Sharing the data is a win-win for us and the vendor.

senses.definition: Someone who talks excessively.
(dated) The lungs.
senses.example: The cold air of that winter got into my windbag and never quite left.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To talk pompously or excessively.
senses.example: He windbagged on about his military service until everyone at the table wanted to leave.

core.definition: A person who talks at great length, often pompously, without saying anything useful or important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowel in 'wind' is short, as in 'windmill', not the long i of the verb 'wind'. The vowel in 'bag' is a clear short a.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It mocks someone's endless or self-important talk, and it is usually said with a laugh among friends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use windbag mostly for a person who talks too much, such as a long-winded politician, a boss who dominates meetings, or a relative who tells endless stories. It is informal and can sound rude if said to someone's face, so save it for friends or public figures. The verb form is rare, so say 'he's a windbag' or 'he talks like a windbag' instead.

distinctions.note: A blowhard boasts loudly about his own achievements, while a windbag simply talks too long and says little.
A chatterbox is cheerful and talks constantly, while a windbag talks at tiresome length in a self-important way.

examples.everyday: Don't invite Mark to the barbecue. He's a windbag and he'll talk about his boat all night.
examples.professional: We need to keep this meeting short, because Jim is a windbag and will spend the whole hour on his slides.
examples.analytical: A critic becomes a windbag when his commentary expands to fill the space without adding any argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a balloon that is mostly air, a windbag fills the room with talk that has little substance inside.
nuance.etymology: Compound of wind (breath, empty talk) and bag, a container; the image is of a bag full of air.
common_mistakes: Using windbag as a neutral word; it is an insult, so do not use it to describe a polite speaker.
Pronouncing the first syllable with the long i of the verb wind, which changes the word's sound.

senses.definition: The state of being windy; the state of there being wind.
The state of being winding or twisting; twistiness.

core.definition: The state of being windy, with strong or frequent wind blowing over a place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and both i vowels are short, as in 'win' and 'pin'. The final ness is reduced to nuhs, not a long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes conditions, with a mild negative tone when the wind is unpleasant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use windiness in weather descriptions, such as 'the windiness of the coast', or in forecasts and travel writing. In everyday speech people more often say 'it's really windy' than use the noun. The noun is more common in writing and formal descriptions.

distinctions.note: Gustiness describes sudden bursts of wind, while windiness describes the general presence of wind over time.
Breeziness is pleasant and light, while windiness can suggest strong or unpleasant wind.

examples.everyday: The windiness on the beach made it hard to keep a towel on the sand.
examples.professional: Our outdoor site survey was delayed by the windiness, which made the drone flights unsafe.
examples.analytical: The windiness of the valley has shaped its architecture, leaving houses low and sturdy against the prevailing gusts.

nuance.analogy: Like a constant draft through an old house, windiness is the steady presence of moving air that you notice all day.
nuance.etymology: Formed from windy, from Old English wind, moving air, with the noun ending -iness.
common_mistakes: Using the long i of WINE-dee, which changes the word's vowels.
Using windiness in casual speech where 'it's windy' is more natural.

senses.definition: Having no, or only rudimentary, wings.

core.definition: Having no wings, or having only small, nonfunctional wing structures that cannot be used for flight.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, WING. The ng is a single sound with no g, and the final -less is a reduced, unstressed syllable, so it sounds like 'luhss', not 'lis'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In biology it is purely descriptive, with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wingless' mainly in entomology and biology, for insects such as fleas and some beetles, or for birds that cannot fly. The word is descriptive and neutral. In everyday talk, people more often say 'can't fly' or 'flightless' for birds like ostriches.

distinctions.note: Flightless describes an animal that cannot fly, even if it has wings; wingless describes an animal with no working wings at all.
Apterous is a technical term for wingless insects, used mostly in scientific writing.

examples.everyday: The little bugs in the garden are wingless, so they're probably fleas or ants without wings.
examples.professional: Our pest report lists the wingless species separately because they require different treatment.
examples.analytical: The wingless form of this insect suggests an adaptation to a stable habitat where flight is no longer useful.

nuance.analogy: A wingless insect is like a boat with no sail: the body is there, but the feature that enables the main function is missing.
nuance.etymology: From 'wing' plus '-less', meaning without.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as 'lis' with a short i; the ending is a reduced 'luhss'.
Using 'wingless' for birds that have wings but cannot fly; 'flightless' is the better term.

senses.definition: Not having any wires.
senses.example: The wireless headphones let me hike without tangled cords.

senses.definition: Functioning without an external wired connection.
senses.example: wireless headphones

senses.definition: The medium of radio communication.
senses.example: Only about a hundred years ago, wireless was a new technology.

senses.definition: A wireless connectivity to a computer network.
senses.example: If your wireless stops working, try restarting the router.

core.definition: Connected by radio or other signals rather than by wires or cables, such as wireless headphones or a wireless network.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the second syllable short and light, with the final s sounding like 'ss'. The final -less is unstressed, so it does not sound like 'lace'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests convenience and freedom from cords.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wireless' today mostly for devices and networks, like wireless headphones, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth. As a noun, 'the wireless' for radio is old-fashioned in American English, and people say 'radio' instead. Use 'wireless' when you mean there are no cords, not when you mean an old radio.

distinctions.note: Cordless usually describes a device with a battery and a base station, such as a phone, while wireless describes a connection that uses radio signals.
Wi-Fi is a specific brand name and standard for wireless local networks, while wireless is the general term.

examples.everyday: These earbuds are wireless, so I don't have to deal with cords.
examples.professional: We need to tighten security on the wireless network in the lab before the audit.
examples.analytical: Wireless communication imposes bandwidth constraints that wired systems avoid by design.

nuance.analogy: Like a conversation across a room, carried by the air rather than a string between two cups.
nuance.etymology: Compound of wire and -less, meaning without wire.
common_mistakes: Using 'wireless' for an old-fashioned radio; Americans normally say 'radio'.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'less' with a long e; the final syllable is short.

senses.definition: The formation of beliefs based on an outcome that aligns with one's desires or hopes, while disregarding evidence, rationality, or reality.
senses.example: Telling yourself the stock will double next month is pure wishful thinking, not analysis.

senses.definition: Decision making based on self-delusion.
senses.example: Deciding to skip the audit because the numbers must be fine was wishful thinking.

core.definition: Believing something is true or will happen because you want it to, not because the evidence supports it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on THINK, with a lighter secondary stress on wish. Reduce the 'fuhl' syllable and pronounce the voiceless th clearly.

nuance.connotation: Negative to mildly critical; it suggests self-deception or unrealistic planning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wishful thinking to call out an overly optimistic belief, especially in business, politics, or planning. Saying 'That's just wishful thinking' can sound dismissive, so you may soften it with 'That's a bit of wishful thinking'. A natural reply is 'Maybe, but let's check the numbers'.

distinctions.note: Optimism is a general hopeful outlook; wishful thinking means believing something without enough evidence.
Denial is refusing to accept a known truth; wishful thinking is building a belief on what one hopes.

examples.everyday: Thinking the landlord will fix the heat for free is a little wishful thinking, don't you think?
examples.professional: Our launch plan rests on wishful thinking, since we have no real data on adoption yet.
examples.analytical: Freud treated religious consolation as a kind of wish fulfillment, though theologians dispute whether that charge fits belief in God.

nuance.analogy: It is like a driver who reads the map by where they hope to go rather than where the road actually runs.
nuance.etymology: Compound of wish, the suffix -ful, and thinking.
common_mistakes: Saying 'wishy thinking' or 'wishful think', which are not standard
Using it as a compliment; it is almost always a criticism

senses.definition: Dead; deceased.
senses.example: My mother, rest her soul, is with God now.

core.definition: Dead; a religious euphemism meaning that someone has passed into God's presence.

pronunciation.tip: The 'th' in 'with' is voiced before a vowel-like sound, and the final 'd' of 'God' is barely released, so it sounds almost like 'gahd' with the sound stopped.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to comforting; it softens the news of a death and is mostly used by religious speakers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this at funerals, in sympathy notes, and when talking about a relative in a church setting. In a secular conversation it can sound unexpected, so people usually say 'passed away' or 'died' instead. A natural reply is a simple sympathy phrase such as 'I'm so sorry for your loss.'

distinctions.note: 'Passed away' is the everyday, secular euphemism; 'with God' carries an explicit religious belief and is best used with people you know share it.
'With the Lord' is nearly synonymous and common in Protestant churches; 'with God' is slightly more general and can be used by any believer.

examples.everyday: My grandmother passed in her sleep last night, and I know she is with God now.
examples.professional: I'm sorry to share that our colleague's father has died, and his family asked us to keep them in our prayers, since he is with God.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'with God' in funeral liturgy expresses a theological claim about the continuing relationship between the dead person and the divine, not merely a polite way of saying someone died.

nuance.analogy: Like a porch light left on for someone who has gone home: the phrase points to a safe destination rather than an ending.
nuance.etymology: 'With' from Old English 'wið' (against, with) and 'God' from Old English 'god'.
common_mistakes: Using it in a secular or workplace setting where 'passed away' would be more natural.
Saying 'to God' instead of 'with God' when describing the dead person's location.

senses.definition: Canis lupus; the largest wild member of the canine subfamily.
senses.example: A lone gray wolf tracked the elk herd along the ridge at dusk.

senses.definition: Any of several related canines that resemble Canis lupus in appearance, especially those of the genus Canis.
senses.example: Ecologists studied the Ethiopian wolf, a rare canine that looks like a fox.

senses.definition: A man who makes amorous advances to many women.
senses.example: Everyone at the office knew he was a wolf who flirted with every new hire.

senses.definition: Any very ravenous, rapacious, or destructive person or thing; especially, want; starvation.
senses.example: They toiled hard to keep the wolf from the door.

senses.definition: One of the destructive, and usually hairy, larvae of several species of beetles and grain moths.
senses.example: Farmers found wolves tunneling through the stored barley, destroying the grain.

senses.definition: A white worm which infests granaries, the larva of Nemapogon granella, a tineid moth.
senses.example: Granary wolves infested the sacks of stored wheat, ruining the entire harvest.

senses.definition: A wolf spider (Lycosidae spp.).
senses.example: A wolf spider darted across the garden path with a cricket in its jaws.

senses.definition: A willying machine, that uses willow twigs to cleanse wool.
senses.example: The mill used a wolf to cleanse the raw wool before carding.

senses.definition: A wolf tone or wolf note.
senses.example: The soft violin solo was marred by persistent wolves.

senses.definition: To devour; to gobble; to eat (something) voraciously.
senses.example: The kids wolfed down three slices of pizza before the game even started.

senses.definition: To make amorous advances to many women; to hit on women; to cruise for sex.
senses.example: At the reunion, he wolfed around the room, hitting on every single woman he saw.

senses.definition: To hunt for wolves.
senses.example: Hunters were allowed to wolf in the northern counties until the quota was filled.

core.definition: A large wild canine that lives and hunts in packs, found in North America, Europe and Asia. Also, a man who flirts aggressively with many women.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short, like the oo in good or wool, not the long oo in food. Pronounce the final f as a clear, voiceless f with no added vowel, and don't add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the animal; negative for a predatory person. As a flirtation term, it can be playful among friends but is insulting when aimed at someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wolf for the animal in everyday speech, nature writing, and wildlife news. The sense of a man who flirts aggressively is informal and often humorous, as in the phrase wolf whistle. Calling someone a wolf can sound flirtatious or rude, depending on tone and relationship, so be cautious.

distinctions.note: A coyote is smaller, slimmer, and has a narrower snout and lighter build than a gray wolf.
A dog is a domesticated animal; a wolf is a wild animal and is generally larger and more heavily built.

examples.everyday: We heard a wolf howling somewhere up the ridge last night, and the dogs went crazy.
examples.professional: The state wildlife office tracks wolf packs in this region with GPS collars and reports the data every spring.
examples.analytical: The wolf in medieval fable stands for appetite and predation, and moral teaching tries to tame it through the figure of the shepherd.

nuance.analogy: A wolf is like a skilled hunter who works best in a team, reading the herd and waiting for the weakest animal to separate from the rest.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wulf, from Proto-Germanic wulfaz.
common_mistakes: Using the long oo vowel from food instead of the short vowel from good.
Forming the plural as wolfs; the plural is wolves, with an f changing to v.
Using wolf for a dog or a coyote, which are different animals.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the wolf is usually an image of danger, violence, or predatory leadership. The Hebrew word is ze'ev and the Greek word is lukos, meaning wolf. Genesis 49:27 describes Benjamin as a ravenous wolf, a picture of fierce tribal strength. Matthew 7:15 warns that false prophets come in sheep's clothing but are inwardly ravenous wolves, meaning they seek to exploit the flock. Isaiah 11:6 pictures a peaceable kingdom in which the wolf shall dwell with the lamb, showing the reversal of violence under God's reign.

wolf.etymology: Middle English *wolf*, from Old English *wulf*, *ƿulf*, from **wulf*, from Proto-Germanic **wulfaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **wĺ̥kʷos*.

senses.definition: Professional experience.
senses.example: The applicant had impressive grades, but no relevant work experience.

core.definition: Professional experience gained through paid or unpaid jobs, used to show your skills to employers.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'SPEER' in 'experience,' and the first syllable 'ex' reduces to 'ik.' Keep 'work' with lighter stress before it.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Having work experience is generally seen as an advantage on a resume or in an interview.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'work experience' in job applications, resumes, and interviews, as in 'Tell me about your work experience.' In everyday talk, people more often say 'I have experience in marketing' or 'I've worked in sales for five years.' On a resume, the section is often called 'Experience' or 'Work Experience.'

distinctions.note: 'Experience' alone is broader and can cover life events, skills, or practice; 'work experience' specifically refers to employment.
Expertise is deep, specialized knowledge or skill, while work experience is the record of time spent doing a job.
Qualifications include degrees, certificates, and licenses; work experience is one kind of qualification.

examples.everyday: My daughter is looking for a summer job so she can get some work experience before college.
examples.professional: The position requires three years of work experience in data engineering, so please list your projects in your resume.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether work experience alone shapes professional judgment, or whether reflection on that experience matters more.

nuance.analogy: Work experience is like a set of miles on a car: the number alone says little, but it shows how far the vehicle has really been driven.
nuance.etymology: Work from Old English weorc; experience from Latin experientia, trial or practice.
common_mistakes: Using 'experiences of work' or 'work's experience' instead of 'work experience.'
Saying 'I have many works experiences'; 'work experience' is uncountable, so say 'a lot of work experience.'

senses.definition: One who works: a person who performs labor for a living; traditionally, especially, manual labor.
senses.example: The factory workers voted to form a union after months of unsafe conditions.

senses.definition: A nonreproductive social insect, such as ant, bee, termite, or wasp.
senses.example: Each colony has thousands of workers that forage for food and tend the young.

senses.definition: A thread performing one instance of a particular task within a program.
senses.example: This FTP client spawns a separate worker for each file to be uploaded.

senses.definition: (rare) A female ant, bee, termite or wasp.
senses.example: The hive's workers are all sterile females that forage and defend the colony.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A person who does paid work for an employer, especially manual, service or hourly labor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, WURK, with the r in both syllables pronounced. The final -er is a reduced schwa with r color, not a full 'ur' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can suggest hard work and dignity, and in political talk it can signal solidarity with ordinary people.
nuance.usage_note: Worker is very common in American news and everyday speech, especially for hourly, manual or service jobs. In HR and corporate writing, people usually say 'employee', and for professionals they say 'staff' or 'professional'. Americans say 'a hard worker' to praise someone's effort.

distinctions.note: Employee is a formal HR term for someone hired by an employer, while worker is broader and more common in everyday speech.
Laborer refers specifically to manual labor and sounds more old-fashioned, while worker covers any paid work.
A contractor is an outside party or self-employed person hired for a task, while a worker is generally someone doing work for pay.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a construction worker, so he's up before sunrise every single day.
examples.professional: We need to make sure our frontline workers get the new safety training before the holidays.
examples.analytical: Debates over the gig economy force us to ask what legally and morally distinguishes a worker from an independent contractor.

nuance.analogy: A worker is like the engine in a factory: the building and machines matter, but production depends on the people running them.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wyrcere, from work plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with the vowel of 'walk' or 'wok', rather than the American 'WURK' with the r sound.
Assuming worker means only manual labor; in American English it can describe any paid worker, including office staff.
nuance.biblical_note: The key Greek word is ergatēs, meaning worker or laborer, from ergon meaning work. Matthew 9:37-38 describes the harvest as plentiful and the workers as few, and Jesus asks the disciples to pray for workers to be sent out. Matthew 20:1-16 tells of workers hired at different hours who all receive the same wage, which the parable uses to show God's generosity. Luke 10:7 and 1 Timothy 5:18 state that a worker deserves his wages, a principle later applied to those who serve in ministry.

senses.definition: Damaged due to continued or hard exposure or use until no longer effective or useful.
senses.example: There is no challenge in fighting a worn-out old man.

senses.definition: Of a person or animal: exhausted or fatigued from exertion.
senses.example: The worn-out soccer players lined up to congratulate the other team.

core.definition: Exhausted from effort, or damaged and no longer useful because of long use.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on OUT, and 'worn' is weaker. The vowel in worn is the 'aw' of 'born,' and the n is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Negative; suggests shabbiness, damage, or deep tiredness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'worn-out' for shoes, tires, or machines, and for a tired person. For people it is informal; 'exhausted' is stronger. Hyphenate it before a noun ('worn-out jeans'), but after a verb write 'worn out' without a hyphen ('These shoes are worn out').

distinctions.note: Tired is general and mild; worn-out suggests you are completely depleted or the object is past repair.
Threadbare describes fabric rubbed thin; worn-out covers any object or a person.

examples.everyday: I'm totally worn out after moving all those boxes.
examples.professional: The server is worn out and needs replacement before the holiday traffic arrives.
examples.analytical: The metaphor of a worn-out faith suggests devotion that has lost its vitality through routine rather than doubt.

nuance.analogy: Like a path worn into the grass by years of footsteps, now bare and no longer green.
nuance.etymology: From 'wear' (Old English werian) plus 'out'; 'worn' is the past participle.
common_mistakes: Writing 'The shoes are worn-out' with a hyphen after the verb
Using it for a person in formal writing, where 'exhausted' is more precise

conversation.text: I'm worn out from moving boxes all day.
The kids are worn out after the birthday party.
These shoes are completely worn out. I need new ones.

senses.definition: Inducing worry.
senses.example: The latest blood test results are worrying, so the doctor wants more tests.

senses.definition: The act of worrying or harassing somebody.
senses.example: Stop the worrying, Mom, I'm fine and I'll call you tonight.

core.definition: Causing worry; making you feel concerned or anxious about something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ing' ending is short and quick. The middle syllable is a light 'ee' sound, so avoid saying 'wor-ree-ing' with a British vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes something that causes anxiety, such as news, symptoms, or silence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use worrying for things that cause concern, like 'worrying news' or 'a worrying sign.' It is the most common and natural form of this group of words in everyday speech. Phrases like 'It's worrying that...' are common in news and conversation.

distinctions.note: Worried describes the person who feels concern, while worrying describes the thing causing the concern, so 'a worried parent' but 'a worrying silence'.
Alarming suggests sudden danger and shock, while worrying describes a milder but ongoing concern.

examples.everyday: It's worrying that the check engine light has been on all week.
examples.professional: The worrying trend in our support tickets suggests the new release is confusing customers.
examples.analytical: It is worrying that many modern accounts of human freedom leave no room for sin, which the biblical writers take seriously.

nuance.analogy: Like a flashing check-engine light: it does not stop you right away, but you should look into it.
nuance.etymology: From worry (verb) plus the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am worrying' to mean 'I am worried' when you feel anxious yourself.
Using worrying for a person who is anxious, when worried is the correct word for the feeling.

senses.definition: An amount or length measured in yards.
The use of a yard, or the fee charged for it.
Territory.
senses.example: The explorers mapped the vast yardage of the uncharted northern plains over three seasons.

core.definition: A total length or amount measured in yards, or the cost of using a yard of material.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, YARD. The r is pronounced and colors the vowel, and the final -age is a reduced 'ij' sound, not 'ahj'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain measurement word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use yardage mostly in two settings: sewing and fabric shopping, where you ask how much yardage a project needs, and sports, especially football and golf, where yardage counts distance gained or the length of a hole. In everyday talk, people more often say 'how many yards' than use the noun yardage, so yardage sounds specific and a bit technical.

distinctions.note: Yards is the plural unit itself, while yardage is a total or an amount measured in yards, so you say 'total yardage' but not 'total yards' for the quantity of fabric.
Footage uses feet and is usually used for film or video length, whereas yardage is used for cloth, golf courses and football.

examples.everyday: How much yardage do you need for those curtains, do you know?
examples.professional: Our quarterback finished the season with the highest total passing yardage in the conference.
examples.analytical: Raw yardage can mislead a comparison between teams unless it is adjusted for the number of plays each team ran.

nuance.analogy: Yardage is like the total amount of ribbon you cut from a spool: it measures how much you used, not the spool itself.
nuance.etymology: Formed from yard (unit of length) and the suffix -age, indicating a quantity or total.
common_mistakes: Saying 'yardage' with a flat, short a, as in 'yad-age'; the first vowel is a broad r-colored ahr sound.
Using 'yardage' for a single measurement; it usually means a total or a number of yards.

senses.definition: A descendant of Zebulun, tenth son of Jacob.
A descendant or member of the tribe of Zebulun.
Of or pertaining to Zebulun, or to the tribe of Zebulun.

core.definition: A descendant of Zebulun, or a member of the tribe of Zebulun in ancient Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ZEB, and give a lighter secondary stress to the final '-nite'. The middle syllables are reduced, so 'yuh' and 'luh' should be short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in biblical studies and historical writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Zebulunite mainly in Bible study, seminaries and historical writing, not in everyday talk. In normal conversation people say a member of the tribe of Zebulun or a descendant of Zebulun. The adjective Zebulunite is used for things related to the tribe, such as territory or leaders.

distinctions.note: Israelite is the broad term for all descendants of Jacob, while Zebulunite names one specific tribe.
Levites were a priestly group without a territorial tribal inheritance, while Zebulunites belonged to a tribe that received territory.

examples.everyday: At our Bible study tonight, someone asked which tribe the Zebulunites were, and I had to look it up.
examples.professional: In my lecture on the tribal settlement, I mention the Zebulunites because their territory helps explain the northern pattern.
examples.analytical: Ezekiel's land allotment places the Zebulunites among the northern tribes, which bears on how tribal boundaries were understood.

nuance.analogy: Think of a Zebulunite as a member of one branch of a large family tree, where Israelite names the whole tree and Zebulunite names one branch.
nuance.etymology: From Zebulun, the Hebrew name Zevulun, with the suffix -ite denoting a member of a group.
common_mistakes: Confusing Zebulunite with Zebulun, which is the name of the ancestor and the tribe.
Using Zebulunite for any Israelite, when it refers only to members of one tribe.
Misplacing the stress, saying zeb-yuh-LOO-nite or similar.
nuance.biblical_note: Zebulun was the tenth son of Jacob and the sixth son of Leah, and the tribe that descended from him received land in Galilee. The Hebrew name Zevulun is explained in Genesis by a wordplay on the root meaning to dwell, though its exact meaning is uncertain. Key passages: Genesis 30:20 gives the naming of Zebulun, linking the name with Leah's hope that her husband will dwell with her. Genesis 49:13 is Jacob's blessing, which says that Zebulun will dwell by the shore and be a haven for ships. Joshua 19:10-16 describes the territory allotted to the tribe of Zebulun in the land of Israel.
